title: Hold Me Tight: Seven Conversations for a Lifetime of Love
source_note: Book text not read. Demon dialogues confirmed by several secondary pages; Hold Me Tight conversation and A.R.E. rest on the author's general knowledge of the book. DB title is 'İlişki Psikolojisi'; the book is Hold Me Tight.

facts.claim: Hold Me Tight (2008) by Sue Johnson is built on seven conversations. The first is about recognising the 'demon dialogues', patterns that trap couples.

Johnson's Emotionally Focused Therapy was formulated and tested with Les Greenberg in 1985; she later integrated attachment theory, which she treats as the defining theory of adult love. The problem is placed in the reinforcing cycle between partners, not in one partner.

Three demon dialogues. Find the Bad Guy: partners go in a circle blaming each other, each defending themselves. Protest Polka: one partner reaches out and protests the disconnect, the other withdraws and pushes back against perceived criticism. Freeze and Flee: follows the polka; the pursuing partner has given up, both step back, and the result is icy silence with no connection.

Johnson frames the pursuer's protest as an attachment protest: in effect the partner is asking whether they matter to the other. The page's image: one person knocking on a brick wall, hoping the other will open it.

Suggested response: treat the pattern as a shared enemy and stay with the present moment; both partners learn to recognise each other's desperation. The connection may be 'forgotten' rather than gone.
EFT's stages: de-escalate the negative cycle; restructure the bond by accessing disowned needs and emotions, accepting the other's experience and expressing needs; then consolidate new cycles.

The book's 'Hold Me Tight' conversation (conversation four) is where a partner, from a softened, vulnerable position, asks directly for what they need instead of attacking or retreating. The book frames the key attachment question as whether the partner is accessible, responsive and engaged (A.R.E.).

facts.claim: A 2019 meta-analysis (Beasley and Ager) found EFT significantly improves relationship satisfaction, with gains sustained up to two years.

EFT's first couples manual was published in 1988. Johnson's nine-step model has three stages (de-escalation, restructuring the bond, consolidation). Attachment styles as described: anxious partners seek reassurance and may use blame, avoidant partners tend to solve problems dispassionately (Johnson and Sims 2000).
